bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;"><strong>In this episode</strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1fa27a5b-a1f4-4919-a0de-902d26c1d17e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Thuan Pham</a><span> was Uber’s first and longest-serving CTO, and today he’s the CTO of Faire, a B2B wholesale platform. Back when Thuan joined Uber, it had around 40 engineers and 30,000 rides per day, and the system crashed multiple times a week. Over seven years, he helped rebuild the system, move it from a monolith to microservices, and scaled the engineering organization behind it. </span><em><span>I had the privilege of working with Thuan for four of those seven years. Later, the very first issue of The Pragmatic Engineer newsletter was a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b78da17f-6b6e-4981-a0d3-2d3f067f94bc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">deepdive into Uber’s Program and Platform split</a><span>. This episode of the podcast contains a nice “full circle” moment, where Thuan shares even more details about why Uber chose to embrace that structure.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We discuss what it takes to operate and build in that kind of environment. Thuan explains how he divided his time at Uber into three “tours of duty,” from stabilizing a fragile system, to re-architecting it, and scaling the org.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We go deep into the platform-and-program split, the Helix app rewrite, and what it took to launch Uber in China in just five months (the original estimate was 18 months). We also cover Uber’s in-house tools and explain why they were necessary to support rapid growth.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Finally, we discuss his role today as CTO of Faire, how the company is using AI, and how he sees AI changing software engineering.</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.375em;"><strong>Key observation from Thuan</strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">14 takeaways from Thuan that I find the most interesting:</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/1d41f4e2-2690-4ba6-8f7e-19d4c669565c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/3jjRNVfm3V4" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>1. Your professional reputation is a compounding asset that pays off unpredictably</strong><span>. Bill Gurley recruited Thuan to Uber based on knowing him from a startup a decade earlier. Similarly, when Thuan needed to hire for critical infrastructure teams at Uber, he reached out to engineers at VMware whom he’d previously worked with, and they followed him to the ridesharing app because they trusted him.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>2. The program/platform split came before microservices</strong><span>. The concept of cross-functional “program” teams and dedicated “platform” teams became necessary because an org split across backend, frontend and mobile engineers slowed down in execution speed when Uber grew to around 100 engineers. Every feature required negotiating bandwidth across the mobile, backend, and dispatch teams. Thuan, Travis Kalanick, and Jeff Holden literally used color-coded sticky notes with people’s names to reorganize into self-sufficient teams. We cover more about this split in the deepdive, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b78da17f-6b6e-4981-a0d3-2d3f067f94bc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Platform and Program split at Uber.</a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>3. Microservices at Uber were more about surviving hypergrowth than anything else.</strong><span> Uber needed to decompose its massive monolith called “API.” To do so, a simple rule was applied: anything new needed to be built outside of the monolith so that no team blocked another. Teams started to build microservices, but decomposing the monolith took a good two years. Fun fact: in 2026, Uber has somewhat fewer microservices (around 4,500) than back in 2016 (around 5,000).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>4. When retiring a monolith, sometimes it gets even bigger before shrinking.</strong><span> After Uber decided to pull services out of the massive monolith, it still kept growing because the business kept adding features! There was an ugly middle phase before the monolith started to shrink. Keep this in mind if you look into decomposing a monolith.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>5. Expect multiple rewrites during hypergrowth.</strong><span> The right architecture depends on how fast a product and company are growing. At Uber, repeated rewrites were common because each one “bought” another window of survival for the company. Thuan’s recommendation is to understand that a rewrite simply means a company is outrunning its existing architecture: this is not necessarily a bad thing!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>6. Controversial launch advice: start with the hardest launch first. </strong><span>When Uber rolled out in China, Travis insisted on starting with Chengdu, the </span><em>largest</em><span> launch city. Looking back, it was scary but also helpful, as launching in the “hardest” city first gave the team confidence and made subsequent city launches much easier.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>7. Travis Kalanick spent 30+ hours interviewing Thuan. </strong><span>This took place over two weeks, as a series of one-on-ones. The sessions became a simulation of working together: disagreeing, aligning, and working things out. I’ve yet to hear of such an intense – and technical! – recruitment process by another CEO.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>8. Uber is the only major company that had a “Senior 1” and “Senior 2” level – and Thuan is unapologetic.</strong><span> Thuan introduced the Senior 1 (L5A) and Senior 2 (L5B) levels because the jump from senior (L5) to Staff (L6) became very big, and larger than between previous levels. One problem this split level created was that Uber’s L5B was akin to Google’s and Facebook’s L6/E6. Thuan resisted the title inflation of just renaming L5B to ‘Staff’.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>9. Name your services clearly; you don’t work at a “Mickey Mouse shop.” </strong><span>As Uber grew more complex, whimsical service names (like “Mustafa”) made navigating systems more tricky, and onboarding for new joiners more painful. Thuan sent a company-wide email which called for professional-sounding naming conventions, and reminded everyone that Uber was not a “Mickey Mouse shop.” The email didn’t fully solve the issue, but did force the growing org to take itself more seriously.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>10. Great engineering talent is global, so bring the opportunity to developers. </strong><span>During Thuan’s time, Uber opened nine engineering offices worldwide in order to access world-class talent. For example, the relatively small Denmark office built and operated core parts of Uber’s infrastructure, such as the trip datastore, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/050d93d0-4691-48fe-b7f7-55e4e64d3edb?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Schemaless</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>11. What’s the most important part of a CTO’s job? </strong><span>Thuan thinks that it’s to build a high-talent-density team, and to “see around the corner” 18–24 months in advance. As he puts it: “your team handles the six-month problems, while you figure out what the organization needs to look like two years from now.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>12. The hardest use case of AI in software engineering is building new features on legacy codebases. </strong><span>At Faire, Thuan’s team uses “swarm coding” (orchestrated AI agents working in parallel) and some engineers there have doubled their output in three months. But generating greenfield code is easy; the real challenge is dealing with millions of lines of code and building features on top with all those existing dependencies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>13. AI raises the floor, but doesn’t change what makes engineers great. </strong><span>AI enables people who can’t code to produce decent apps, but great engineers are still finding ways to leverage AI tools and accelerate even more. The differentiators remain the same as before AI: curiosity, fearlessness, and a willingness to innovate and learn new things.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>14. Thuan’s career advice: think of it in phases. </strong><span>Each segment of your career has different priorities, which Thuan sees like this:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">First 5–10 years: seek maximum learning and push yourself hard.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Mid-career as a senior/staff engineer: seek roles to make an outsized impact in, perhaps at a smaller company.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">In leadership roles: teach and coach others, and bring them along with you.</p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Datadog’s Metrics Summary page had a problem. For one customer, every time someone loaded the page, the database had to join a table of 82,000 active metrics with 817,000 metric configurations. The p90 latency hit 7 seconds. Every time a user clicked a filter, it triggered another expensive join.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The team tried the usual fixes, such as query optimization, indexing, and tuning. However, the problem wasn’t the query. They were asking a database designed for transactions to do the job of a search engine. Fixing that one page set off a chain of architectural decisions that didn’t just solve the performance issue. It led Datadog to fundamentally redefine how data replication works across its entire infrastructure.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">In this article, we will look at how Datadog implemented the changes and the challenges they faced.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from the Datadog Engineering Team. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">The Database Was Simply Doing the Wrong Job</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Datadog operates thousands of services, many of them backed by a shared Postgres database. For a long time, that shared database was the right call. Postgres is reliable, well-understood, and cost-effective at small to medium scale. However, as data volumes grew, the cracks started to show, and the Metrics Summary page was just the most visible symptom.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The team’s first instinct was to optimize the database. They tried adjusting join order, adding multi-column indexes, and using query heuristics based on table size. None of it held up and there were several issues:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">Disk and index bloat slowed inserts and updates.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">VACUUM and ANALYZE operations added maintenance overhead.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">Memory pressure drove up I/O wait times.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Monitoring with Datadog’s own APM confirmed that these queries were consuming a disproportionate share of system resources, and getting worse as the data grew. By the time multiple organizations crossed the 50,000-metrics-per-org threshold, the warning signs were everywhere, such as slow page loads, unreliable filters, and mounting operational overhead.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">See the diagram below:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" justify">Postgres was being asked to do two fundamentally different jobs at once. OLTP workloads are what relational databases are designed for. However, real-time search with filtering across massive denormalized datasets is a completely different workload, one that search engines like Elasticsearch are purpose-built to handle.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Therefore, instead of making Postgres better at searching, Datadog stopped making it search at all. They replicated data from Postgres into a dedicated search platform, flattening the relational structure into denormalized documents along the way. The mechanism behind this is Change Data Capture, or CDC.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Postgres already records every change (every insert, update, and delete) in its Write-Ahead Log, or WAL. This log exists primarily for crash recovery, but it can also be read by external tools. Datadog used Debezium, an open-source CDC tool, to read that log and stream changes into Kafka, a durable message broker. From Kafka, sink connectors pushed the data into the search platform.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The advantage of this approach is that the application itself didn’t need to change how it wrote data. It still writes to Postgres as before. However, search queries now hit the search platform instead, which was purpose-built for exactly that workload.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Why Async?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Before scaling that pattern, the team faced a key design choice: synchronous or asynchronous replication.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">In synchronous replication, the primary database doesn’t confirm a write to the application until every replica has acknowledged receiving it. This guarantees strong consistency, meaning every system has the same data at all times. But it’s slow. If one replica is across the network or temporarily unhealthy, the entire write pipeline stalls waiting for confirmation. One slow consumer becomes a bottleneck for everything.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Asynchronous replication flips this. The primary database confirms the write immediately, and replicas catch up afterward. The application never waits for downstream systems. This is faster and more resilient, but it introduces a window where the replica is behind the source. This gap is what’s known as replication lag. The data will get there, but not instantly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">See the diagram below:</p><div justify">Datadog chose async. At their scale, with thousands of services spread across multiple data centers, synchronous replication would have coupled their application’s performance to the network latency and health of every downstream consumer. That was a non-starter.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">One factor that helped in the decision-making was the cost being concrete. For a brief window after a write, the search platform might show slightly stale results. If a user adds a new metric configuration and immediately searches for it, the search platform might not have the update yet. For Datadog’s use cases (search, filtering, analytics dashboards), a few hundred milliseconds of lag was a perfectly acceptable tradeoff compared to 7-second page loads.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Debezium captures changes from the WAL, and Kafka acts as a durable buffer between the source and all consumers. Since Kafka persists messages to disk and supports replay, changes aren’t lost even if a consumer goes down temporarily. The consumer just picks up where it left off.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This tradeoff between consistency and availability shows up everywhere in distributed systems. It’s a practical instance of the CAP theorem, which describes the fundamental tension between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Async replication solved the performance problem. However, it introduced a new challenge. What happens when the shape of your data changes?</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">The Problem With Schema Evolution</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">In a normal application, changing a database schema is between you and your database. You run a migration, add a column, change a type, and move on. With CDC, every schema change propagates to every downstream consumer, and if those consumers aren’t ready for the change, the pipeline breaks.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Let us consider a concrete example. A team adds a required region field to a table using ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET NOT NULL. Debezium starts producing messages that include this field. But messages already sitting in Kafka were written under the old schema and don’t have it. Consumers expecting every message to have a non-null region field start failing, and the pipeline goes down.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Datadog built a two-part defense against this.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The first line of defense is an automated validation system that analyzes schema migration SQL before it’s applied to the database. It catches risky changes, like adding NOT NULL constraints, and blocks them from being deployed without coordination. Most migrations pass through automatically. The ones that don’t get flagged require the team to work directly with the platform team to coordinate a safe rollout.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The second line of defense is a multi-tenant Kafka Schema Registry configured for backward compatibility. This means any new schema must still be readable by consumers that only understand the old schema. In practice, this restricts schema changes to safe operations, such as adding optional fields or removing existing ones. When Debezium captures an updated schema, it serializes the data in Avro format and pushes both the data and the schema update to the Registry.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" Registry checks the new schema against the existing one and either accepts or rejects it based on the backward compatibility rules. Datadog uses Avro serialization specifically because it supports this kind of schema negotiation natively. The Confluent Schema Registry documentation covers the mechanics of backward, forward, and full compatibility modes.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Together, these two systems mean that most schema changes flow through automatically, breaking changes get caught early, and downstream consumers don’t wake up to broken pipelines.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">With async replication running and schema evolution under control, Datadog had a working pipeline. However, setting up each new pipeline still required an engineer to manually configure seven or more components across multiple systems. That’s where automation changed the game.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">From One Pipeline to a Platform</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">A single CDC pipeline involves a number of moving parts. For example, you need to enable logical replication on Postgres by setting wal_level to logical. Also, you need to create Postgres users with the right permissions, establish replication slots and publications, deploy Debezium instances, create Kafka topics with correct mappings, set up heartbeat tables for monitoring, and configure sink connectors to push data into the destination.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Doing all of that manually for one pipeline is tedious. But doing it across many pipelines and multiple data centers means the operational burden compounds quickly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">See the diagram below:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 If a step fails, the workflow retries or rolls back cleanly. Teams don’t touch infrastructure directly. They request a pipeline through the platform, and the automation handles everything end-to-end.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;text-align: justify">Conclusion</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Every architectural choice Datadog made came with a cost:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">Asynchronous replication means downstream systems are always slightly behind the source.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">Schema evolution constraints mean you can’t freely change your database without considering the pipeline.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The infrastructure itself (Debezium, Kafka, Schema Registry, Temporal) represents a lot of moving parts to operate, monitor, and maintain.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">Lastly, building all of this into a platform requires a dedicated team to own it.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This approach makes sense when you have workloads that genuinely don’t belong in your primary database, when multiple teams need the same data in different shapes, and when your scale makes manual pipeline management untenable. Datadog checked all three boxes. However, if you have a handful of simple data flows, the overhead isn’t justified. A periodic batch sync or a straightforward read replica might be all you need. Not every problem requires a platform.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><strong>References:</strong></p><ul style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>Two years ago, we learned about </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d8aebe68-3548-45d2-b01c-27506cd641e0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">how LLMs work</a><span> at a high level from </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d8aebe68-3548-45d2-b01c-27506cd641e0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">the ChatGPT team</a><span>, and today, almost all software engineers use large language models (LLMs) in our day-to-day work. The most visible part of using an LLM is </span><strong>inference</strong><span>; when an existing model takes an input (prompt) and generates an output, one token at a time. So, with AI models and AI agents everywhere across the tech industry in 2026, that means so is inference.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>And now, inference engineering is becoming more widespread, too, as open LLM models grow more capable. </strong><span>This is because with closed models, inference engineering is done only by the AI engineers who build the model, whose number might add up to a few thousand globally. In contrast, with the open models which tech companies are adopting, it’s possible to tweak them to perform better at inference. For example, Cursor built its new Composer 2.0 model </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b0e2b69f-ec8d-487f-ba34-8b8b1522a5fc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">on top of</a><span> the open Kimi 2.5 model, and successfully used plenty of inference engineering approaches to make it even faster.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So, based on this industry-wide prevalence and the related need for superior technical performance, it’s worth understanding a bit about what inference engineering actually is, and some interesting approaches worth knowing about, as a software engineer.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For some answers, I turned to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/efea12e3-2661-4f9e-96bb-4c29efdcd295?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Philip Kiely</a><span>, a software engineer who has been working for four years at the inference startup, Baseten. With his hard-earned experience, Philip has written an excellent, in-depth book about precisely this topic, </span><em>“Inference Engineering.”</em></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: Engineering</em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In today’s issue, we cover:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Setting the stage: why is inference so important? </strong><span>More capable, widespread, open models are driving demand for inference engineering.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>What is inference? </strong><span>As the phase that comes after training a model, the inference layer introduces new engineering challenges like batching, caching, and quantization.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>When is inference engineering needed?</strong><span> Investing in this area is typically worth it when your product and usage scales up, and there are product requirements which a current, off-the-shelf solution lacks.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>What hardware does inference use? </strong><span>Datacenter GPUs are the most common, while on-premises, air-gapped GPUs are also employed.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>What software does inference use? </strong><span>Commonly-used software includes NVIDIA’s CUDA and Dynamo, as well as hardware-agnostic projects like PyTorch, vLLM, and others, which are growing in popularity.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>What infrastructure does inference need? </strong><span>Autoscaling is a baseline requirement. Kubernetes is a popular choice for autoscaling inside a cluster, while multi-cloud inference might be necessary for high-scale use cases.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Five approaches to make inference faster. </strong><span>Quantization (reducing the numerical precision of a model’s weights), speculative decoding (taking advantage of spare compute to generate “draft tokens”), caching, parallelism (tensor parallelism and expert parallelism) and disaggregation (separating the prefill and decode phases to run on separate workers, not the same GPU).</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This deepdive uses a few abbreviations and concepts that are everyday lingo for inference engineers, but maybe are not for those less versed in the domain:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>CUDA: </strong><span>Compute Unified Device Architecture. NVIDIA’s proprietary API to program NVIDIA GPUs for high-performance computing, including LLM-related use cases.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>TTFT</strong><span>: time to first token. Think of this as the “time to process the prompt.” This metric determines the perceived responsiveness of models and GenAI systems.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>TPS</strong><span>: tokens per second. Akin to a model’s “typing speed.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>ITL</strong><span>: intertoken latency. The time between generating one token and the next.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>KV cache</strong><span>: key-value cache. The cached results of the attention algorithm, reused between requests to speed up inference. </span><em><span>We cover more on KV cache in the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e6d7f625-8049-43cc-bfd1-f0d507e878ae?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Scaling ChatGPT deepdive</a><span>.</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Prefill / decode: </strong><span>the two phases of inference. Prefill is when the model takes the full input and processes tokens, outputting the KV cache. Decode is the phase in which the model generates one token at a time.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>MoE</strong><span>: Mixture of Experts. An architecture that enables models to be pretrained with far less compute. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b00061e4-9f0e-4da3-839f-bb9561630380?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">More details on this approach.</a></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Below is an introduction to inference adapted from Philip’s book, “</span><em>Inference Engineering,” which </em><span>is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0cd0f2c6-d54d-42a8-bcab-65fafd0b738c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">free to download as an e-book</a><span>. Physical copies are currently sold out, but Philip is printing more as fast as possible.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>My usual disclaimer: as with all my recommendations, I was not paid to mention this book, and no links in this article are affiliates. See my </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f5551e55-5648-46dd-9551-f0171aca6aa6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">ethics statement</a><span> for more.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>With that, it’s over to Philip:</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;">1. Setting the stage: why is inference so important?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Inference is the most valuable category in the AI industry, but inference engineering, on the other hand, is still in its infancy. In their work, inference engineers work across the stack from CUDA to Kubernetes in pursuit of faster, less expensive, and more reliable serving of generative AI models in production.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When ChatGPT launched in late 2022, there were perhaps a few hundred inference engineers in the world, and they didn’t call themselves that. These specialists mostly worked at frontier labs like OpenAI, Midjourney, and Anthropic, or at big tech companies like Google and NVIDIA.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Back then, it looked like this might be the way of the AI industry: that training generative AI models would be so hard and expensive that only a handful of companies would develop closed models and thereby require inference engineering for production serving. In that alternate future, the rest of the world would be mere consumers of AI via APIs, renting intelligence a token at a time.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Three years later, it turns out that training generative AI models is indeed both hard and expensive – but it’s not so hard and expensive to be limited to a handful of players. Instead, a proliferation of open models – more than two million and counting on </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bf1bea5e-14d1-4e5f-9c7d-acc92bb99321?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Hugging Face</a><span> (the “GitHub for AI”) – means that today every engineer can now deploy their own intelligence to power AI products.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Research labs around the world, from OpenAI and NVIDIA Nemotron in America, to Mistral AI and Black Forest Labs in Europe, to Alibaba Qwen, DeepSeek AI, Z AI, and Moonshot AI in China, regularly release open models of all modalities.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px open models is accelerating, which differ by the availability of their weights:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Closed model: </strong><span>A proprietary model whose weights are unavailable to the public, like GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Open model: </strong><span>A model whose weights are publicly available, like Llama or DeepSeek, and which is usually released under the MIT license, or a similar permissive license (some models restrict commercial use, so always double-check license terms).</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Before December 2024, there was a meaningful gap in intelligence between closed and open models, but when DeepSeek V3 and R1 were released, that gap disappeared. </span><em><span>Note from Gergely: we previously covered </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0e2e411b-3ef0-4464-99fc-8558d98f731e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">how DeepSeek’s release rocked the AI industry.</a></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Today, new closed models are matched by open models within months if not weeks, and occasionally, open models like Kimi K2 Thinking even exceed closed models’ capabilities for brief periods.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Despite the fact that open models are constantly chasing closed models on benchmarks, they nonetheless change the equation for AI product builders. And as both types improve, closed and open models cross capability thresholds.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure define the industry today. But over time, closed models got smarter and new categories like customer service voice agents and AI-powered IDEs became possible. The early models were slow, expensive, and unreliable, but the capabilities were there and AI engineers began building companies around them.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>As open models crossed the same capability thresholds, these folks began using them to replace closed models.</strong><span> Many also began fine-tuning open models to cross capability thresholds faster, and even exceed closed model quality in their specific product and domain.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" and economics</em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Switching to open models means the opportunity to use inference engineering to make the models powering AI products better in new ways:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Latency:</strong><span> Closed model APIs are built for throughput, but open models can be optimized for real-time applications.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Availability: </strong><span>While APIs for GPT and Claude are stuck at two nines of uptime, it’s possible to achieve four nines or better with dedicated deployments of open models.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Cost:</strong><span> Open models are often at least 80 percent less expensive at scale.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So, whereas three years ago it looked like inference engineering was a niche field, the fact is that today, every company aiming to build truly differentiated and competitive AI products needs an inference strategy.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">AI-native startups like Cursor, Clay, Gamma, and Mercor are redefining hypergrowth by building products that rely on open and in-house models. Leading digital native companies like Notion and Superhuman succeed by deeply integrating AI capabilities into their category-defining products.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Elsewhere, a new generation of blended research and engineering teams – World Labs, Writer, Mirage, and dozens more – are building businesses by training and productizing their own foundation models.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Adoption is even strong in enterprise and regulated industries, which historically were slow to adopt new technologies. Companies like OpenEvidence, Abridge, and Ambience are making generative AI ubiquitous in healthcare, while at the world’s largest companies, AI initiatives are moving past the pilot stage into massive user adoption. Market-wide demand for inference means that everyone from developers to executives has the opportunity to learn inference engineering and use it to advance their career and business.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I’ve been incredibly fortunate to have a front-row seat in the fastest-moving market in history over the last four years at Baseten, where we power mission-critical inference for the best AI products, including every company listed in the previous paragraphs.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>The good news is that you are early. </strong><span>There are still relatively few professionals working on inference, and newcomers can become experts quickly. Also, the potential and impact of inference is becoming ever clearer, but the domain is still in its infancy. That means there are enormous opportunities to solve novel, interesting, and deeply technical problems at all levels of the stack.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;">2. What is inference?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Inference is the second phase of a generative AI model’s lifecycle:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Training:</strong><span> The process of learning model weights from data.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Inference:</strong><span> Serving generative AI models in production.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">During the past decade’s machine learning (ML) boom, hundreds of thousands of data scientists and ML engineers became familiar with the full lifecycle of training and inference for ML models.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Inference for classic ML models is relatively straightforward. In the early days of Baseten, we ran inference for models built with tools like XGBoost on lightweight CPUs with a simple software stack.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In contrast, inference for generative AI models is complex. You can’t simply take model weights, get some GPUs, and expect inference to be fast and reliable enough for large-scale production use. Doing inference well requires three layers:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Runtime:</strong><span> Optimizing the performance of a single model on a single GPU-backed instance.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Infrastructure:</strong><span> Scaling across clusters, regions, and clouds without creating silos, while maintaining excellent uptime.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Tooling:</strong><span> Providing engineers working on inference with the right level of abstraction to balance control with productivity.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">These three layers must work together to create a system that can handle mission-critical inference at scale.</p><div 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;">A complete inference stack includes runtime and infrastructure optimizations</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The runtime layer is responsible for ensuring an individual model running on a GPU (or across several GPUs in a single instance) runs as performantly and efficiently as possible. This layer depends on a sophisticated software stack, from CUDA, to PyTorch, to inference engines like vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. Low-level optimization is important, with kernels like FlashAttention delivering significant performance gains.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The runtime layer relies on a number of model performance techniques that apply new research to the challenges of inference on generative AI models:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Batching:</strong><span> Run incoming requests in parallel, weaving them together on a token-by-token basis to increase throughput.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Caching:</strong><span> Reuse the KV cache – the cached results of the attention algorithm – between requests that share prefixes.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Quantization:</strong><span> Lower the precision of select pieces of the model to access more compute and reduce memory burden.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Speculation:</strong><span> Generate and validate draft tokens to produce more than one token per forward pass during decode.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Parallelism:</strong><span> Efficiently leverage more than one GPU to accelerate large models without introducing new bottlenecks.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Disaggregation:</strong><span> Separate the two phases of LLM inference, prefill and decode, onto independently scaling workers.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">These model performance techniques are used for all modalities and not just LLMs, such as vision language models, embedding models, automatic speech recognition, speech synthesis, image generation, and video generation, which extend the capabilities of AI systems and require their own inference optimizations. But these runtime optimizations are not enough: no matter how performant a single instance of a model server is, it will eventually receive more traffic than it can handle. This is not a CUDA problem or a PyTorch problem, it’s a systems problem that needs to be solved at the infrastructure layer.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The nature of infrastructure problems changes at each level of scale. At first, the problems are around autoscaling: knowing when to add and remove replicas, and figuring out how to do so quickly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Past a certain scale – generally a few hundred GPUs – infrastructure problems are defined by capacity.</strong><span> To get access to enough GPUs, inference engineers begin spreading workloads across multiple regions and cloud providers. This quickly leads to silos, where models in one cluster may be starved for resources while other clusters have unused capacity. The final level of scale in infrastructure is a global system that treats all available resources as a single unified pool of compute.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Thoughtful multi-cloud infrastructure also improves reliability, protecting against downtime in any individual region or cloud provider. And for global applications, running inference near to end users improves end-to-end latency.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Once these runtime and infrastructure capabilities are built, they need to be presented at the appropriate level of abstraction. Inference providers like Baseten and internal teams building inference need to consider what tooling and developer experience to provide as the critical third layer in a complete inference platform.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Of course, developer experience is subjective. For inference, one extreme is the black box: give a platform model weights, and get back an API. At the other extreme is providing only basic constructs for compute, network, disk, and so forth.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The right developer experience is somewhere in the middle, where inference engineers have enough control to run mission-critical inference confidently, and enough abstraction to work productively.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This article – which is an excerpt of </span><em>Inference Engineering</em><span> – presents an overview of the technologies and techniques that power inference across all three layers of runtime, infrastructure, and tooling.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;">3. When is inference engineering needed?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Inference engineering adds speed and scale to AI products by optimizing production serving of generative models. Optimization means identifying the best solution from a range of options.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Before optimizing model performance and building robust infrastructure, you need to know what “best” means for your product; many performance improvements come from making tradeoffs in latency, throughput, and quality. In practice, optimization is often about finding the right balance, rather than maximizing a single factor.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For example, NFL players are big, fast, and strong. But they’re not as big as sumo wrestlers, fast as Olympic sprinters, or strong as champion powerlifters. Their bodies and skills are optimized to fulfill the specific demands of their position over the course of a full season.</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/c79a5b5b-fe14-494d-b672-ae1e95a6ef9c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em>Like elite athletes, inference services must be specialized for the demands of their workloads</em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Similarly, your inference system must be optimized to fulfill the specific demands of your model, product, and traffic. The more constraints you can introduce, the better the outcomes that can be achieved.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">You should know:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Model requirements: </strong><span>Which model(s) do you need to run inference on?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Application interface: </strong><span>How will inputs be delivered to the model, and how is the output expected to be formatted?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Latency budget: </strong><span>How fast does your product need to respond to a user action, end-to-end?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Unit economics: </strong><span>How much sense does it make to spend on a per-request, per-user, or per-month basis?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Usage patterns: </strong><span>How many concurrent users are you serving, and is there any pattern to their usage (e.g., more activity during business hours)?</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Early in building an AI product, the answers to these questions may not be clear. At this point, it’s often better to use off-the-shelf APIs whenever possible, rather than investing in dedicated inference. But as a product scales, the requirements become clear and inference engineering becomes a worthwhile pursuit.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;">4. What hardware does inference use?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Inference engineering relies on accelerators: powerful hardware designed to load terabytes of data and perform trillions of operations per second.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The most common type of accelerator for inference is the GPU, and the market leader in GPUs for inference is NVIDIA. My book focuses on inference engineering for NVIDIA GPUs in the datacenter, and also covers other vendors of datacenter accelerators and local inference.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Across vendors, there are three types of GPUs on the market:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Datacenter GPUs: </strong><span>Racked servers with interconnected high-performance GPUs. Example: NVIDIA B200.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Workstation GPUs: </strong><span>Individual desktop GPUs for professional workflows. Example: NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Personal computing GPUs: </strong><span>Individual desktop GPUs for everyday use. Example: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Inference at scale uses datacenter GPUs mounted on racks: refrigerator-sized chassis with standardized power, networking, and cooling.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Datacenter GPUs like the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/36d845ee-5eeb-42a1-8078-808b6b019c7c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">NVIDIA B200</a><span> offer the highest individual performance, and more importantly, include high-bandwidth GPU-to-GPU interconnects, are installed in highly standardized configurations, and are available by the millions in datacenters worldwide.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I doubt there is a B200 GPU running under your desk, but if there is, please send me a picture! Instead, inference on datacenter GPUs runs in one of three modes:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Cloud: </strong><span>GPUs are rented in someone else’s datacenter, usually hyperscalers like AWS and GCP, or neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>On-premises: </strong><span>GPUs are purchased and installed in a datacenter that you control directly.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Air-gapped: </strong><span>GPUs are installed on-prem and you need to physically access the GPUs to run inference.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Most inference engineers use cloud GPUs. Large enterprises and governments run on-prem and air-gapped deployments, but cloud-based GPUs offer the flexibility and access that fast-growing AI products need to scale.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Even with constraints, navigating the hardware landscape is complex. From variations between cloud providers, to NVIDIA’s personal naming conventions, there are many nuances in selecting the right accelerator.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;">5. What software does inference use?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">NVIDIA’s market dominance in the inference space is in no small part due to the robust, mature software ecosystem around its hardware. Hardware iteration cycles are slow. Best-in-class hardware companies like Apple and NVIDIA release new architectures and generations at most annually, with two-year release cycles being more common. But software iteration is fast. Often, to run a newly released open model on day zero, you need to install a nightly build or other pre-release version of each software dependency just to get support for the new model.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Software’s fast iteration cycle and lower barrier to entry dramatically expands the landscape of inference engineering. There are countless companies building software at various levels of the inference stack, in contrast to hardware, which centers on NVIDIA and a few competitors.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For inference engineers, these are some of the key software players:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>NVIDIA:</strong><span> Invests heavily in its own sometimes-proprietary software ecosystem, from CUDA up to Dynamo.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Hugging Face:</strong><span> Maintains a model registry for all open models plus </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b5cf862e-864f-4853-b712-2a54258c88e0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">transformers</a><span> (models built on the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d45ad182-e703-44fc-8e88-6647cc002712?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">transformer architecture</a><span>), and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/403d93b8-8831-4368-aea3-841ac6a5f811?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">diffusers</a><span> (models built on the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1c0fc910-29bb-45eb-917c-3bc4713848c1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" rel="" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">diffusion-based</a><span> generative ones).</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>The Linux Foundation:</strong><span> Maintains hardware-agnostic projects like PyTorch and vLLM.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>LMSYS Org:</strong><span> Develops essential tools for inference and evaluation, most notably SGLang.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There are thousands more companies, universities, and research institutions making essential open-source contributions to inference. Over time, technologies have been built at increasing levels of abstraction:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>CUDA: </strong><span>Direct communication to the GPU for explicit control over computations and memory.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Deep learning frameworks: </strong><span>Abstractions over CUDA for training, exporting, and running neural networks in Python.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Inference engines: </strong><span>Highly configurable PyTorch-backed inference for common architectures.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>NVIDIA Dynamo: </strong><span>Sits on top of inference engines to power large-scale deployments.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Most inference engineering today happens at the higher levels of abstraction, configuring and deploying inference engines and orchestrating inference across multiple GPUs. No matter which level of the stack you work at, it’s essential to have a strong mental model for the adjacent levels of abstraction to guide your work.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: 1.625em;">6. What infrastructure does inference need?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When you scale production traffic, your assumptions are rigorously tested. Everything from input and output sequence lengths, to traffic patterns, to what topic a user decides to chat about; they all impact your observed performance in production. And maintaining secure, robust infrastructure is an entirely different skillset from optimizing model inference on the GPU.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">No matter how fast and efficiently a single instance can serve a model, the service will be overwhelmed if traffic gets high enough. It’s an infrastructure problem, not with PyTorch or CUDA, and it requires a different mindset and different technologies.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Scaling in production introduces new complexities about where and how to get GPUs, balance traffic across them, and prevent downtime. The goal of autoscaling is to ensure you always have enough resources to serve all incoming requests, while maintaining latency SLAs and without wasting money on idle GPUs.</p><div
